strengths: The paper is built on a clear, well-supported empirical observation: MOTR contains a strong hidden detector whose signal is suppressed when track queries are active (Tab. 1: 60.0 to 66.3 AP, Fig. 2). This is demonstrated cleanly and motivates the rest of the work.

The systematic comparison of four detection-prior injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) in Tab. 2 is a genuinely useful controlled study that isolates which mechanism matters and how each affects detection vs. association metrics.

SelfMOTR is a conceptually clean, detector-free, fully end-to-end design that decouples proposal generation from the tracking pass by reusing the model's own detection-only output as 4D anchor proposals. This removes the external-detector dependency of MOTRv2/MOTRv3 while preserving the end-to-end character.

The experimental analysis is thorough: cumulative component ablations (Tab. 5), proposal-source and threshold ablations (Tab. 6, 8), detection-association conflict quantification (Tab. 9), decoder-depth analysis (Fig. 5), and runtime profiling (Tab. 10).

On DanceTrack test the method is competitive (69.2 HOTA, 72.5 IDF1) and achieves the highest association score among end-to-end methods, consistent with the claimed better feature-space alignment between detection and tracking queries.

The paper is clearly written, the motivation is well articulated, and the detection-association conflict is quantitatively demonstrated (AP drop of 6.3 for MOTR vs. 0.3 for the self-proposal variant).
weaknesses: The headline empirical gains are modest. On DanceTrack SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) does not surpass CO-MOT (69.4), and on MOT17 SelfMOTR (57.5 HOTA) is slightly below the MOTR baseline (57.8), so the method does not clearly advance the state of the art on either benchmark.

The central novelty—replacing frozen external detector anchors with the model's own detection-pass proposals—yields only marginal benefit over the already-strong 4D Anchor Proposal variant (Tab. 6: 58.2 vs. 58.0 HOTA, 80.0 vs. 79.2 MOTA). The paper itself concedes these are comparable, which undercuts the strength of the 'self-generating priors' claim.

The core insight is incremental relative to prior work. The detection-association conflict and the value of detection priors are already established (CO-MOT, MOTRv2/MOTRv3); the contribution is a specific integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper acknowledges the conflict was 'explicitly addressed' in follow-up work.
The dual-pass design adds compute (20.7 vs. 24.8 FPS, ~17% slower) and requires running the decoder twice, which is a non-trivial cost for the small accuracy gains obtained.

Evaluation is limited to two benchmarks and only the MOTR baseline; the paper does not study integration with stronger query-based architectures (CO-MOT, MOTRv3), leaving the generality of the approach unverified.

The abstract's claim of 'competing with recent state-of-the-art' is honest but reflects parity rather than improvement; combined with the MOT17 regression, the practical value proposition over existing detector-free trackers is not strongly established.

strengths: Clear and well-supported diagnostic insight: the paper empirically demonstrates (Fig. 2, Tab. 1, Tab. 9) that MOTR-like trackers contain a 'hidden' detector whose detection accuracy is suppressed once track queries are activated, with mAP rising from 60.0 to 66.3 when track queries are removed at inference. This is a genuinely useful observation for the MOT community.

The systematic study of four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) in Tab. 2 provides a well-organized empirical dissection of how detection priors can be leveraged, and the findings (e.g., anchor proposal giving the largest standalone gain) motivate the proposed method.

SelfMOTR is a conceptually clean and fully end-to-end, detector-free design: it generates self-proposals from a detection-only pass with shared weights and feeds them into the tracking decoder, removing reliance on external detectors while keeping the pipeline compact. The dual-pass design with a shared heavy encoder is efficient (20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS, Tab. 10).

The ablation suite is thorough and informative: proposal source (Tab. 6), data scaling (Tab. 7), proposal threshold (Tab. 8), detection-association conflict (Tab. 9), and decoder-depth analysis (Fig. 5) collectively support the design choices.

The conflict analysis in Tab. 9 is a strong quantitative demonstration that the proposed design practically removes the detection-association conflict (AP drop of -0.3 vs. -6.3 for MOTR), which is a meaningful and well-evidenced claim.

The paper is clearly written, with a logical flow from the motivating analysis to the method and ablations, and limitations (only instantiated on MOTR-style baseline; only DanceTrack and MOT17) are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The headline results are only on par with prior work rather than clearly advancing the state of the art: on DanceTrack, SelfMOTR achieves 69.2 HOTA vs. CO-MOT's 69.4 HOTA (Tab. 3), and the paper itself describes the result as 'on par.' The claimed advantages (highest AssA among end-to-end methods) are relatively narrow.

On MOT17 (Tab. 4), SelfMOTR (57.5 HOTA) does not improve over the MOTR baseline (57.8 HOTA), which weakens the generality of the central claim that exposing hidden detection capability robustly improves tracking; the paper attributes this to detector-aligned training of competitors but does not fully substantiate the 'detector-sensitive benchmark' framing.

The methodological novelty is incremental: the core mechanism (a detection-only pass producing 4D anchor proposals fed into the tracking decoder) is conceptually close to the anchor-proposal strategy of MOTRv2 and related prior-injection approaches; the main delta is generating proposals internally rather than from a frozen external detector. The paper acknowledges this similarity but the resulting contribution is a refinement rather than a new paradigm.

Evaluation is limited to two datasets (DanceTrack and MOT17), and the method is only instantiated on the MOTR baseline, not on stronger query-based architectures such as CO-MOT or MOTRv3. The paper explicitly notes this as a limitation, which leaves the generality and scalability of the self-proposal mechanism unverified.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports: e.g., the assertion that the detection-association conflict is 'practically removed' rests on a single validation-set AP comparison, and the efficiency claim of 'only a modest runtime overhead' comes with a ~17% FPS reduction that could matter for real-time applications.

The relationship to existing analyses of MOTR's detection-only inference is not fully disentangled; the paper should more clearly delineate which parts of the 'hidden detector' observation are novel versus previously reported, to sharpen the originality claim.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, well-quantified empirical observation that MOTR's detection capability is suppressed by track queries (Fig. 2, Table 1: 60.0 → 66.3 mAP when track queries are removed), and Table 9 shows the same conflict persists during training (AP drops 66.3 → 60.0 with track queries). This analysis is systematic and useful.

The comparison of four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) in Table 2 is a reasonable empirical study that isolates which mechanism is most effective, and the finding that anchor-proposal reuse yields the largest standalone gain is informative.

The proposed SelfMOTR is simple, detector-free, and preserves the end-to-end character of MOTR, requiring only a second lightweight decoder pass. Runtime overhead is modest (20.7 vs 24.8 FPS, Table 10), and the decoder-depth study (Fig. 5) justifies the shallow proposal generator.
The ablation suite is fairly thorough, covering proposal source, confidence threshold, data scaling, and the detection-association conflict, and a limitations paragraph is included.
Writing is clear and the method and experimental protocol are described with enough detail (optimizer, batch size, clip length, QIMv2 module) to be plausibly reproducible.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The central 'key insight' that MOTR is a strong hidden detector is explicitly attributed to prior work ([23] CO-MOT), and the proposed remedy — running a detection-only pass and converting detections into 4D anchors/queries — is conceptually a self-generated variant of MOTRv2's external-anchor-proposal injection. The delta over existing detector-free methods (CO-MOT shadow queries, MOTRv3) is incremental.

The main results do not establish an advantage over prior art. On DanceTrack (Table 3) SelfMOTR reaches 69.2 HOTA vs. CO-MOT 69.4 and MOTRv3 68.3, i.e., essentially tied, while using additional training data (CrowdHuman/HSV) and an added denoising stage borrowed from prior work. On MOT17 (Table 4) SelfMOTR is 57.5 HOTA, which is actually below the MOTR baseline (57.8) and well below CO-MOT (60.1) and MOTRv3 (60.2). The claim of 'competing with state-of-the-art' is therefore only weakly supported, and the method does not robustly improve across datasets.

There is internal inconsistency in the evidence chain. The validation ablations (Table 5) top out at 64.4 HOTA after adding HSV+CrowdHuman and denoising, yet the test-set number reported is 69.2 HOTA. It is never made explicit which configuration produces the headline 69.2 result, and the gains attributed to 'self proposal' are entangled with added data and the denoising stage imported from prior work, complicating attribution.

Several reported differences are within noise (e.g., ±0.3 HOTA in Table 3/Table 5, Self Proposal 58.2 vs. 4D Anchor Proposal 58.0 in Table 6), which undermines strong claims such as 'the detection-association conflict is practically removed' (Table 9) being presented as a headline finding rather than a single, potentially fragile measurement.

The distinction between the final SelfMOTR design (confidence-modulated proposal queries) and the 'Anchor Proposal' ablation is blurry, and the paper does not clearly separate the contributions of the 4D-anchor positional component versus the confidence-modulated content embedding, so it is unclear which design choice drives the reported gains.

The limitations section is brief and acknowledges that the method is only instantiated on MOTR-style architectures; given that MOTRv3 and CO-MOT already occupy this design space with better results, the paper does not convincingly argue why this particular instantiation is the right point in the design space or what it enables beyond the existing alternatives.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: the paper first empirically establishes that MOTR retains hidden detection capacity by showing (Fig. 2) that disabling track queries at inference yields consistently higher and more stable mAP, then builds a mechanism directly on this observation.

The proposed SelfMOTR is simple, fully end-to-end, and detector-free, yet well justified: a detection-only pass produces self-proposal queries (4D anchors + confidence-modulated content) that are concatenated with propagated track queries, decoupling proposal discovery from association while keeping a single shared decoder and a joint training objective.

Thorough and honest ablation study: four prior-injection strategies (Table 1), proposal-source comparison (Table 7), proposal confidence threshold (Table 4c), decoder depth (Fig. 6), data scaling (Table 4b), and a cumulative component analysis (Table 6). The detection-association conflict ablation (AP 66.3→60.0 for MOTR vs. 71.2→70.9 for SelfMOTR) is a compelling, quantitative demonstration that the interference is largely removed.

Competitive empirical results: leading end-to-end HOTA of 71.1 on BFT and strong AnimalTrack results (45.5 HOTA), plus the highest association score (59.3 AssA) among end-to-end methods on DanceTrack. These gains are reported on genuinely challenging, diverse domains (dance, bird flocks, animals), not just a single benchmark.

The Track Attention Mass diagnostic, together with normalized Shannon entropy, provides a novel and interpretable lens on joint decoding, and is analyzed layer-wise (Fig. 5a), token-wise (Fig. 5b), and across datasets (Fig. 7). It connects a mechanistic hypothesis to an architectural fix.

Efficiency is addressed: the heavy encoder is run once, the extra cost is a shallow second decoder pass, and the paper reports 20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS for an anchor-based MOTR variant, with evidence that detection/tracking saturate after a few decoder layers.

The limitations section (Appendix A, MOT17) openly reports that end-to-end methods, including this one, still lag non-end-to-end pipelines and that clip-length tuning only helps detection, which is a useful and non-defensive discussion.
weaknesses: The core idea is incremental with respect to prior work: MOTRv2 already exploits detection priors for MOTR and CO-MOT already notes that removing track queries improves detection. The novel element is generating those priors internally rather than importing them, which is a sensible but modest conceptual step. The paper itself acknowledges that the anchor-proposal variant (using a frozen detection-pretrained MOTR) already reaches 58.0 HOTA on DanceTrack val, essentially matching the self-proposal variant (58.2), so the 'self-generating' aspect yields limited additional accuracy over simply reusing a detector.

Much of the headline DanceTrack gain does not come from the proposed mechanism. Table 6 shows self-proposals alone raise HOTA from 51.2 to 58.2, while HSV augmentation plus CrowdHuman joint training raise it to 64.3 and denoising to 64.4. The paper argues data scaling is better exploited after decoupling (Table 4b), which is a reasonable defense, but the reported test-set number (69.2) still mixes several ingredients and makes attribution of the improvement to the proposed contribution difficult.

The claims of state-of-the-art are qualified but still somewhat overstated. On DanceTrack test, SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) is below CO-MOT (69.4), MOTRv2 (69.9), MeMOTR (68.5 is lower but MOTRv2/MOTRv3 are higher), and DetA (80.9) is below CO-MOT (82.1). The statement that the method 'achieves state-of-the-art performance' on BFT is dataset-specific, and the assertion that internal prior generation should be a 'default design principle' for unified tracking is stronger than the evidence supports, especially given MOT17 results that do not exceed non-end-to-end baselines.

The attention-based analysis is largely correlational. The 'healthy regime', 'sink-like behavior', and 'contextualization phase' interpretations are plausible but not rigorously validated: there is no controlled experiment (e.g., directly regularizing attention statistics) demonstrating that the attention distribution causes the performance difference rather than co-varying with it. Entropy thresholds such as ~0.85 are asserted as healthy without a principled criterion.

Some comparisons are incomplete or potentially unfair. Baselines in Tables 2 and 3 are drawn from different codebases with different backbones, training data, and augmentation regimes (the paper marks backbone mismatch in gray only in Table 5). A controlled comparison against a MOTR baseline trained with identical HSV/CrowdHuman/denoising settings but without self-proposals would isolate the contribution more cleanly.

The two-pass inference introduces a real cost that is only partially quantified. The speed comparison is against 'MOTR with learnable 4D anchors' (24.8 FPS) rather than against the standard MOTR pipeline, and no FLOPs or latency breakdown of the proposal pass versus the tracking pass is given, so the practical overhead of the dual-pass design remains somewhat opaque.

Reproducibility details are reasonable but incomplete: several hyperparameters (e.g., c_prop = 0.05, lambda_prop = 0.5, N_learned = 10) are ablated or fixed, yet the paper does not discuss how sensitive the final results are to the number of appended learned anchors, the proposal-count cap N_prop, or the choice of a detection-only pass depth at test time in a fully specified manner.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and well-motivated diagnosis of the detection–association conflict in end-to-end transformer trackers, and the empirical observation that MOTR retains substantial latent detection capacity when track queries are disabled (Fig. 2) is a useful and clearly presented finding.

The proposed Track Attention Mass diagnostic, borrowed from the attention-sink literature in LLMs, is a novel and interpretable analytical lens for joint-decoding trackers; the layer-wise and token-level analyses in Figs. 5–7 add mechanistic insight beyond simple benchmark comparisons.

The ablation study in Table 1 is systematic and informative: it isolates four distinct prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) and shows that explicit 4D anchor proposals are the most effective, which cleanly motivates the final design.

The method is conceptually simple, detector-free, and fully end-to-end, avoiding the re-introduction of external detectors that has characterized MOTRv2/MOTRv3/CO-MOT. The self-proposal formulation is a sensible design principle for unified tracking.

Results on Bird Flock Tracking (71.1 HOTA, new SOTA among end-to-end trackers) and AnimalTrack are strong and demonstrate generalization to challenging, non-pedestrian domains; the runtime analysis (20.7 FPS) and decoder-depth study (Fig. 6) are practical and welcome.
The paper is clearly written, with well-organized ablations, confidence intervals on key metrics, and honest discussion of the MOT17 limitations in the appendix.
weaknesses: On DanceTrack — the primary benchmark — SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) is essentially on par with CO-MOT (69.4 HOTA) and remains well below graph-based methods (e.g., NOOUGAT 68.4, SUSHI 63.3 HOTA are actually lower, but the claim of 'highly competitive' is weakened by the absence of a clear margin over the closest detector-free baseline). The improvement over CO-MOT is within noise, so the headline claim is not strongly supported on the main dataset.

The core observation motivating the method — that MOTR's detection capability is suppressed by joint decoding and can be recovered in a detection-only pass — is explicitly attributed to CO-MOT [25] in the manuscript. The paper's own contribution is therefore largely the mechanism for exploiting this known observation, which reduces the perceived novelty.

The novelty relative to MOTRv2 (anchor proposals from a frozen detector) and CO-MOT (shadow queries) is incremental: SelfMOTR replaces the external/frozen source with the model's own detection-only pass. While the distinction is real, it is a relatively small architectural step, and Table 1 already shows the frozen-detector anchor proposal variant is the strongest ablation — meaning self-proposals mainly remove the external dependency rather than producing a large accuracy gain.

On MOT17 (Table 5), SelfMOTR (57.5/58.4 HOTA) is notably below CO-MOT (60.1) and even MOTRv2 (57.6) on some metrics. The authors frame this as a general limitation of end-to-end tracking, but it does weaken the case that self-generated priors are broadly superior.

The 'detector-free' claim is somewhat semantic: the model is initialized from COCO-pretrained Deformable DETR weights, and the method still requires a separate detection-only decoder pass at inference. The efficiency comparison (20.7 vs 24.8 FPS) shows the dual-pass design is slower than a single-pass MOTR baseline, so the practical cost of the decoupling is not negligible.

The causal link between balanced Track Attention Mass and improved tracking is argued but not directly established — no intervention experiment (e.g., explicitly regularizing attention balance) is provided to show that the attention shift causes the performance gain rather than merely correlating with it. The analysis is largely post-hoc.

The optimal proposal threshold c_prop = 0.05 (Table 4c) is very low, effectively retaining nearly all detections; this raises questions about how selective the 'confident' proposal filtering actually is and whether the proposal-quality argument is as strong as claimed.

Reproducibility details are mostly present, but the paper does not report variance over multiple seeds for the main DanceTrack result (only the ablations carry error bars), which matters given the narrow margin over CO-MOT.

strengths: The empirical observation that MOTR's detection capacity is suppressed by track queries (Fig. 2) is a clean, well-documented finding that directly motivates the method and is independently useful for the community.

The systematic ablation in Table 1 comparing four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) is a genuinely informative study, with the anchor-proposal variant showing the largest standalone gain.

The self-proposal formulation (detection-only pass → 4D anchors + confidence-conditioned content embeddings → concatenated with track queries) is simple, cleanly described, and yields strong results on BFT (71.1 HOTA, SOTA) and competitive DanceTrack numbers.
The Track Attention Mass diagnostic, while descriptive, provides an interesting quantitative lens on query interference and is supported by layer-wise and distributional analyses (Figs. 5, 7).

Ablations are thorough: detection–association conflict measurement (Table 4a), data-scaling (Table 4b), proposal threshold (Table 4c), and component accumulation (Table 6) collectively give a reasonably complete picture.
Runtime overhead is modest (20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS for MOTR) and the decoder-depth analysis (Fig. 6) justifies a shallow proposal pass.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core mechanism is essentially running MOTR's detection branch with track queries disabled and reusing its outputs as anchors, which is conceptually close to DAB-DETR learnable anchors, CO-MOT shadow queries, and MOTRv2 external anchors. The contribution over prior 'decouple detection from association' work is incremental.

On the primary benchmark (DanceTrack), SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA, 80.9 DetA) does not clearly surpass CO-MOT (69.4 HOTA, 82.1 DetA); the detector-free framing does not translate into a detection or tracking advantage, yet the framing of the contribution is stronger than the evidence warrants.

MOT17 results (Table 5) are notably weak (57.5/58.4 HOTA), well below CO-MOT (60.1), MOTRv3 (60.2), and most non-end-to-end methods. This directly undercuts the paper's claim that internal prior generation should be a 'default design principle for unified tracking,' and the discussion is relegated to the appendix rather than confronted in the main text.

The causal story around Track Attention Mass is speculative ('we hypothesize'), resting on correlational distributions. The analogy to LLM attention sinks is loose, and the metric is a bespoke cardinality-corrected ratio whose connection to downstream tracking quality is not established beyond post-hoc description.

The reported gains appear partly attributable to auxiliary components (HSV augmentation, joint CrowdHuman training, QIMv2, denoising) that competitors already use; Table 6 shows self-proposals alone move DanceTrack val HOTA 51.2 → 58.2, with most of the remaining jump coming from data/augmentation rather than the proposed mechanism.

The proposal filtering via confidence threshold is shown to be nearly inert: the best setting (0.05) keeps essentially all detections, and the threshold ablation shows minimal differences, so the 'selection' component is not doing meaningful work.

Reproducibility signals are weak: the project page URL is truncated, no code repository is linked, and key training details (e.g., the composition of the 'small fixed set of learned proposal anchors,' stability of the two-pass training, sensitivity to λ_prop) are not fully specified.

The central claim of 'practically removed' detection–association conflict (Table 4a, AP 71.2 → 70.9) is a diagnostic result whose downstream tracking impact is not isolated from the auxiliary training changes; the connection between this metric and the reported HOTA gains is asserted rather than demonstrated.
